highlights.text: As I reread what I wrote yesterday, it occurred to me to wonder if my character began to change the day my husband, jokingly, began calling me “mamma.” I liked it a lot at first, because it seemed to imply that I was the only adult in the house, the only one who knew about life. That increased my sense of responsibility, which is something I’ve always felt, since childhood. I also liked it because it allowed me to justify the impulse of tenderness roused in me by Michele’s manner, which has remained candid and ingenuous, even now that he’s almost fifty. When he calls me “mamma” I respond in a tone that’s severe yet loving, the same I used with Riccardo when he was a child. But now I see that it was a mistake; he was the only person for whom I was Valeria.
I have to recognize that, perhaps, the determination with which I protect myself from any possibility of rest is the fear of losing this single source of happiness, which is tiredness.

Yesterday, too, at Giuliana’s, I had the impression that we moved in different worlds, almost that we spoke a different language. I looked at them with amused curiosity, as one watches a performance. I don’t really know how to explain my impression, but, well, it seemed to me that they had remained stuck in our school years, and that, of all of us, I alone had grown to adulthood. Eager to be young again, I tried to imitate them. I made an effort to remind myself that we’re nearly the same age, we have a lot of shared memories, we’re all married, have children—so our problems should be the same.

I didn’t know how to explain our differences, which I feel grow more profound every year. I admit that I tried to understand them, while they were talking, as when I first arrived at the school and tried to follow when they spoke rapidly in French. Camilla humorously described the Christmas presents her husband had given her, expensive gifts she’d managed to get by means of astute and elaborate maneuvers. She wore a small hat decorated with a gray bird of paradise that fascinated me. Giuliana also explained how she had induced her husband to buy her a piece of jewelry. They were very entertaining—it was like watching magic tricks.

During those two hours, it had been as if they were acting in a play in which I alone didn’t know my part, I had forgotten the lines. I was silent and gradually I understood that the unbridgeable gap that has opened between us in recent years is due to the fact that I work and they don’t. Or, more precisely, to the fact that I am capable of contributing to the financial needs of my life and they aren’t.

Now, under everything I do and say, there’s the presence of this notebook. I never would have believed that everything that happens to me in the course of a day would be worth writing down. My life always appeared rather insignificant, without remarkable events, apart from my marriage and the birth of the children. Instead, ever since I happened to start keeping a diary, I seem to have discovered that a word or an intonation can be just as important, or even more, than the facts we’re accustomed to consider important. If we can learn to understand the smallest things that happen every day, then maybe we can learn to truly understand the secret meaning of life. But I don’t know if it’s a good thing, I’m afraid not.
It’s terrible to think that I sacrificed my entire self to beautifully perform tasks that they consider obvious, natural.

But maybe it’s hard to maintain friendships for a lifetime no matter what. In reality, at a certain moment, each of us changes, becomes different, some go forward, others remain fixed, and thus we move in opposite directions, so there’s no longer a meeting place, no longer anything in common. I would have liked to call Clara Poletti, I thought, as I transcribed her name, at least to wish her happy holidays. The fact is that I don’t have time: I have less and less time. It even seemed pointless to put her number in the new book; we almost never see each other anymore, not since she separated from her husband.

Maybe I wanted this notebook in order to tell the tranquil story of our family: maybe that’s what impelled me to buy it. I would have liked to reread it when the children were married and we were alone, Michele and I. Then I would have been able to show him the notebook proudly, as if, unbeknownst to him, I had stored up a patrimony for our old age. It would have been lovely. Instead, since I began writing, not everything that happens in our house seems to me pleasant to recall.

Sometimes I think I’m wrong to write down everything that happens; fixed in writing, even what is, in essence, not bad seems bad. I was wrong to write about the conversation I had with Mirella when she came home late and, after talking for a long time, we separated not as mother and daughter but as two hostile women. If I hadn’t written it, I would have forgotten about it.

We’re always inclined to forget what we’ve said or done in the past, partly in order not to have the tremendous obligation to remain faithful to it. Otherwise, it seems to me, we would all discover that we’re full of mistakes and, above all, contradictions, between what we intended to do and what we have done, between what we would desire to be and what we are content to be.

My mother and I talk only about material things, things far from what is truly important to us: she’s always been cold toward me; even when I was a child she seldom hugged me and when she did it increased my awe. She sent me to boarding school early. I think her attitude comes from the habitual reserve of her aristocratic family. In fact, she always addressed her mother formally. I had intended to bring up my daughter very differently, to be her friend, her most intimate confidante. I didn’t succeed. I wonder if such an attempt can possibly succeed. And yet yesterday, talking to my mother about material things, the market, the household chores, I realized that through that conventional language we have always talked about what was happening inside us, intimately, not confessing it openly but with an understanding that can exist only between mother and daughter. Yesterday, for example, I felt that when we were saying that, given the price of artichokes, one could no longer go on, we were alluding to something different. And she recognized in me a weariness, a dangerous weakness, when she advised me to get someone to help in the house. I seem to have understood all that only now, maybe because now I, too, have a daughter I can’t understand. Instead I am understanding my mother and, writing about her, I have a desire to bury my head in her shoulder, something I would never dare to do if she were present.

I have to confess that, at first, I wasn’t at all happy about the fraternal relationship that was established between my husband and me, and, in my heart, I reserved some bitterness toward Michele. But I didn’t say anything, afraid, precisely, of seeming ridiculous. I convinced myself that Mirella wasn’t wrong, that I was now an old woman. I will say, rather, that her pitiless, if certainly involuntary, cruelty served to make me accept an undeniable reality more easily.

I need to be alone sometimes. I would never dare confess it to Michele, I’d be afraid of upsetting him, but I dream of having a room all for myself. Even a maid who works all day without stopping says, “Good night,” and has the right to shut herself in a room, in a pantry. I’d be content with a pantry. But I can’t remove myself, ever, and only by giving up sleep can I find time to write in this notebook. If, when I’m at home, I interrupt what I’m doing, or at night, in bed, I stop reading and stare into space, there’s always someone who kindly asks what I’m thinking about. Even if it’s not true, I respond that I’m thinking about the office or that I’m doing some accounts; in other words, I always have to pretend to be thinking about practical things, and this fiction wears me out.

“At a certain age,” he continued, “everything we’ve done is no longer enough. It was useful only in making us what we are. And just as we are, now that we’re truly ourselves, what we’ve wanted to be or could be, we’d like to start to live again, consciously, according to our current tastes. Instead, we have to continue to live the life we chose when we were someone else.
We’ve been married for years, we’re so immersed in each other that, when we’re together, he’s at ease, as if I weren’t there. This thought, which always was a source of consolation, now saddens me.

I wondered if for Michele I’m still a living woman or already, like his mother, a portrait on the wall. So I am for my children. Certainly, so my mother is for me. I wished desperately to escape the evil spell of that portrait.
It’s sad to have given so much of oneself to one’s children to reach the conclusion that the only people they don’t trust is us.

I often have a desire to confide in a living person, not only in this notebook. But I’ve never been able to. Stronger than the desire to confide is the fear of destroying something that I’ve been constructing day by day, for twenty years, the only thing I possess.

Often, in other words, I wonder what the relations between Michele and me have been for years. I feel I should question myself and write at length: it would be too great an effort and so I give it up. But this question has returned insistently ever since I noticed that, even if the thought of another man always occupies my mind, I can still say with sincerity, “I love my husband.” I feel no uneasiness saying it. I’ve often said it to Guido, too. Saying it, I feel protected. In fact, it allows me to listen to everything he says about Venice, not to protest at his first timid kisses, and not to reproach him when he uses the intimate tu, as he’s been doing for two days. I always answer formally, because I don’t want to offend him, or encourage this new intimacy we have. Last night I said to Mirella, “I’ve always loved your father, I still love him,” and didn’t have the impression I was telling a lie. But now I begin to wonder what the word “love” means in reference to Michele, and what feelings am I alluding to when I say, “I love my husband.”

“Those were things of another time that you’re thinking of! You gradually lose the habit of certain things and in the end you don’t think about them anymore.” “There,” I insisted, “you really believe that one doesn’t think about them anymore? Or maybe we no longer dare to be sincere the way we were then?” “How old were we then?” he said. “You know I’m almost fifty? We’re no longer … ” “It’s not true,” I interrupted. “If you mean we’re no longer young, I’ll say you’re wrong. I know it, we’re young: if we don’t compare ourselves to our children, we’re very young.”

At night, when we sit at the table together, we seem transparent and loyal, without intrigues, but I know now that none of us show what we truly are, we hide, we all camouflage ourselves, out of shame or spite.
